findings.title: Findings converge on the write row living only in memory on its pending-reply entry until the reply arrives
findings.why_it_matters: Under D1 and D2, a write's row is built when the call is sent but is held only on its `PendingResponses` entry. It reaches the database only when the reply (or `fail_all`) resolves that entry. Three separate findings from both critics come back to this one mechanism:
findings.choice_reason: Asked why the parent declined recording at send; after the transcript review showed it was only weighed as a cheaper no_reply fix, chose to re-evaluate. Settled: insert at send and update on resolution (D8), startup sweep of stale pending rows (D9), cap raised to 10,000 id-only entries (D2).

findings.title: Service data, event data and helper params are stored verbatim, credentials included
findings.why_it_matters: D3's `data` column holds "the rest of what the caller passed", cut at 2,048 code points. That includes `code=` on `alarm_control_panel.alarm_disarm` and `lock.unlock`, a password-mode `input_text` helper's `initial`, and webhook or API tokens in service data. These values land in SQLite for `retention_days` and in `hassette execution --json`, which is the output people paste into issues. Hassette
findings.choice_reason: Key-name redaction gives a false sense of security. Go with C now; filed #3956 for a SecretStr marker in records and #3955 for Api writes accepting SecretStr.

findings.title: `not_sent` can't be inferred from the exception classes the send paths raise
findings.why_it_matters: D4 calls `not_sent` "the one outcome that's certain". The design leaves the write function to classify from the exception path, and the hierarchy doesn't support that:
findings.choice_reason: Asked whether this comes from Hassette's historically ambiguous exception classes; yes. Filed #3957 to split transport exceptions by delivery state before #3677's build.

findings.title: A cancelled awaited write leaves a sent call with no row
findings.why_it_matters: D1 covers a timeout and D4 covers exceptions. Neither covers cancellation. When a handler is cancelled while awaiting `wait_for_ack`, `return_response`, `fire_event` or a helper write, `CancelledError` (a `BaseException`) skips `mark_timed_out` and any `except Exception` recording path. findings.title: Rejected-call WARNINGs on the receive task are unbounded, and "one WARNING per episode" is undefined
findings.why_it_matters: D7 emits one WARNING per rejected background call on the WebSocket receive task, with `CURRENT_EXECUTION_ID` set around it. An app looping 200 lights against an unavailable integration produces 200 WARNINGs in one burst. Emitting a log record is a non-blocking put on the bounded `HassetteQueueHandler`, so the receive task isn't slowed by log I/O. The senior engineer's delay concern doesn't hold. T

D5 joins only `trigger_context_id` to `api_writes.context_id`, so that run reads `caused_by: None`. findings.choice_reason: Asked whether an automation turning on a watched light is the scenario; clarified it only applies when a Hassette write starts the chain.

findings.title: D2's 2.5 KB-per-entry memory bound ignores the uncut `target`
findings.why_it_matters: D2's "about 2.5 MB worst case" assumes that only `data` is cut, at 2,048 code points. D3's normalized `target` is a JSON object of id lists with no limit, so a call on a large id list, held on a background entry, makes the stated bound false.

findings.title: Findings converge on D1's hand-off of a row's resolution from the awaiting caller to a converted background entry
findings.why_it_matters: Three findings from both critics hit the moment D1 turns an awaited WebSocket write's entry into a background entry, and each asks the design to say who resolves the row and when. Finding 4: the write function has to infer from the exception class whether the converted entry now owns the row, and D4's classes overlap (`ResponseTimeoutError` is also a `FailedMessageError`, which D4 maps to `rejected`). Finding 5: a reply already delivered to the future before the cancel is lost, and the converted entry waits for a reply that never comes. Finding 6: a cancel during `send_json` converts an entry for a frame that may never have been sent. Each one proposes its own patch: a `WHERE outcome = 'pending'` guard, a `fut.done()` check, a "send completed" marker. Together they suggest the problem is the two-owner lifecycle itself: the caller owns the row until some point, the entry owns it afterwards, and that point is defined by which exception the caller saw. Should the hand-off be re-evaluated as one question rather than guarded three times? That includes whether a converted entry is needed at all, and whether some of these cases are limitations to accept and document.
findings.recommended: A: Re-evaluate D1's hand-off before addressing Findings 4, 5 and 6 individually. Open questions: who owns a WebSocket write's row from registration to reply, and does that owner change? Does a caller that stops waiting need to change the entry's kind at all? How does the design tell "sent" from "not sent" and "reply consumed" from "not yet" at the moment the caller stops? Is exactly-once resolution enforced by single ownership or at the database? Which of these cases are worth handling, and which are limitations to document?
findings.choice_reason: A: entry owns the row from registration (correlator pattern), after a prior-art pass on late-reply ownership

findings.title: Findings converge on the terminal state of a row whose resolution was lost
findings.why_it_matters: Both critics landed on what a row says once nothing will ever update it. Finding 7 (senior-engineer): an evicted entry or a dropped update leaves the row `pending` for the rest of a process that can run for weeks. The evicting code knows at that moment that no update will come, yet the row keeps claiming a wait. Finding 8 (data-integrity): D9 then labels those rows `connection_lost`, which D3 defines as "sent, no answer will come", even when Home Assistant did answer and only the record was lost. One field carries both questions: when a row whose resolution was lost leaves `pending`, and what it says when it does. Each local fix (resolve at eviction, add an outcome value, document the overloaded label) settles part of that and constrains the others. Should the terminal state for a lost resolution be decided once rather than finding by finding? That includes whether D2's and D9's ratified acceptances already settle it, and whether this is a limitation to document.
findings.recommended: A: Re-evaluate the terminal state of a row whose resolution was lost before addressing Findings 7 and 8 individually. Open questions: what does `pending` promise a reader during uptime? Which paths know a row will never be updated (eviction, a dropped update, `fail_all` overflow, crash)? Does a lost resolution need its own value, or is `connection_lost` with documentation enough? Should anything change during uptime, or only at startup? Is the ratified acceptance in D2 and D9 the right answer after all?
findings.choice_reason: A: add an `unresolved` outcome for eviction and the startup sweep; connection_lost only from fail_all

findings.title: D9's sweep predicate ("`session_id` isn't the current session's") can't be evaluated where the sweep runs
findings.why_it_matters: D9 puts the sweep in `mark_orphaned_sessions` and words it as every `pending` row "whose `session_id` isn't the current session's". That step runs before `create_session`, so no current session id exists yet. Read literally, the build either reads `SessionManager.session_id`, which raises `RuntimeError` and fails startup through `_fail_startup`, or compares against `None`, where `session_id != NULL` is NULL in SQL and sweeps nothing. A NULL `session_id` row would also never match. The intended behavior holds only because of call order the text doesn't state. The two-processes-on-one-DB case senior-engineer raises is no worse under either wording: the existing orphan UPDATE already assumes one process per DB.
findings.chosen: In D9's Recommendation, replace "The sweep covers every row whose `session_id` isn't the current session's, whether that session ended cleanly or was orphaned" with: "The sweep sets every `pending` row to `connection_lost` (`WHERE outcome = 'pending'`), in the same step as the orphaned-session update and before this process's session is created (`mark_orphaned_sessions` runs before `create_session` in `src/hassette/core/core.py`), so no row of this process exists yet and every `pending` row belongs to an earlier session, whether it ended cleanly or was orphaned." Keep the remaining sentences. Add a build test: pending rows from an earlier session, including one with a NULL `session_id`, are swept at startup.

findings.title: Two paths can resolve one row, and the write function decides which by exception class
findings.why_it_matters: D4 has the write function map `OutcomeUnknownError` to `connection_lost` "unless D1 turns the entry into a background entry". The write function has to work out whether a converted entry now owns the row, and the only signal it has is the exception class. Those classes overlap today. `ResponseTimeoutError` (a converted entry) is both an `OutcomeUnknownError` and a `FailedMessageError`, which D4 maps to `rejected`. `ResponseLostError` (no conversion, the caller resolves) is also an `OutcomeUnknownError`. If the build gets the order or the inference wrong, two updates are enqueued for one row and the later one wins. The critic proposes a `WHERE outcome = 'pending'` guard to make resolution first-writer-wins. On the paths traced here, though, the later writer is usually the reply, which is the truth. A first-writer-wins guard would lock in the caller's wrong early guess (for example `rejected` on a timeout) instead of letting the reply correct it.
findings.recommended: A: In D4's mapping, name the outcome-unknown cases separately. The timeout that D1 converts → the write function enqueues no update, since the entry's callback resolves the row. The connection lost while the caller is still awaiting → `connection_lost`. Check the timeout class before the rejection class.

findings.title: A reply delivered to the future just before a cancel is lost when the entry converts
findings.why_it_matters: `respond_if_necessary` sets the awaited future's result and returns. If the handler task is cancelled (handler timeout, reload) before it resumes, `CancelledError` comes out of `asyncio.wait` with `fut.done()` already true. D1 then converts the entry to a background entry waiting for a reply that has already been consumed. The row stays `pending` until the connection ends. `fail_all` or D9 then records `connection_lost`, though Home Assistant answered, possibly with success. Nothing counts this case.
findings.recommended: A: Add D1's cancel case: if the future already holds a result or exception when the caller is cancelled, resolve the row from it instead of converting, then re-raise.

findings.title: A cancel during `send_json` converts an entry whose frame may never have been sent
findings.why_it_matters: The entry is registered before `await self.send_json(...)`, and D1 converts it on `CancelledError` without saying where in that sequence the cancel landed. A cancel during the socket write (handler timeout, reload) leaves a background entry and a `pending` row for a request Home Assistant may never have received. Nothing resolves it until the connection ends (`fail_all` → `connection_lost`) or the cap evicts it, and with no deadline (parent D7) a stable connection can last weeks. The final label (`connection_lost`, outcome unknown) is roughly right. The cost is the long `pending` and an entry held against the cap. Both critics raised this independently.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a cancel during the socket write leaves the row `pending` until the connection ends or the entry is evicted, then `connection_lost`.

findings.title: Evicted entries and dropped updates leave a row `pending` for the whole uptime
findings.why_it_matters: D2 and D8 both end in "row stays `pending` until D9's sweep", and D9 runs only at startup. Hassette runs for weeks. `pending` on the read can then mean in flight, evicted, update dropped, or HA never answered, and the 2am question "why is this write pending since yesterday" has no answer in the row. At the moment of eviction the code knows no update will come: the reply would be ignored. D2 and D9 ratified this as accepted. What's new is that the evicting code could resolve the row on the spot, an option D2's table didn't weigh. For a dropped update nothing can be retried (Posture), so only a read-side treatment is possible.
findings.recommended: A: At eviction, call the evicted entry's resolve callback with the outcome the D9 sweep writes, and say so in D2.

findings.title: D9 labels answered-but-unrecorded calls `connection_lost`, which asserts no answer came
findings.why_it_matters: D3 defines `connection_lost` as "sent, no answer will come, outcome unknown", and D9 sweeps every leftover `pending` row to it. For crash and shutdown leftovers that's accurate: the connection did end. A row left by a dropped update or an eviction usually did get an answer, often `success` or `rejected`. Labelling it `connection_lost` stores a cause the earlier observation contradicts, and a reader diagnosing a reconnect incident (6 of the parent's 13) can't tell a real connection fault from a lost record. Drops are counted and not retried, and that posture isn't challenged here. Only the label is.
findings.recommended: A: Add an outcome for "sent, resolution not recorded", written by the D9 sweep (and by eviction, if Finding 7's A is chosen). `connection_lost` stays for rows resolved by `fail_all`.

findings.title: D8's insert-lands-first guarantee depends on enqueue order the design doesn't state
findings.why_it_matters: D8 says "FIFO order on the single writer guarantees the insert lands first". That holds only if the insert is enqueued before the request is registered and sent. The entry is registered before `send_json`, and a reply can arrive while the send is still awaiting. If the build enqueues the insert after `send_json` returns, a fast reply's update reaches the queue first, matches no row, and the later insert stays `pending` until restart. The design says "at send", which allows either order.
findings.chosen: In D8's Recommendation, after "FIFO order on the single writer guarantees the insert lands first", add: "provided the insert is enqueued before the request is registered or sent, since a reply can arrive while `send_json` is still awaiting; each write function enqueues its insert first, and a test pins it with a reply that arrives during the send."

findings.title: D2's cap check inherits a whole-table scan, and "oldest" is conversion order for awaited entries
findings.why_it_matters: `mark_timed_out` rescans the whole table on every call, justified by a comment that the cap of 100 makes it cheap. D2 raises the cap to 10,000, adds fire-and-forget entries, and keeps both in one dict. If the build keeps the scan-and-slice shape on each background registration, a table near the cap costs a pass over up to 10,000 entries per call on the event loop. Separately, `mark_timed_out` pops and reinserts, so a converted awaited entry sorts by conversion time, not send time. D2's rationale ("a call waiting longest is the one most likely still running a long script") describes send order, which the code doesn't implement for converted entries.
findings.recommended: A: Add to D2 that eviction order is the order entries became background entries (send order for fire-and-forget, conversion order for awaited), reword the "waiting longest" rationale to match, and require that the cap check not rescan the table per registration, with a 10,000-entry test.
findings.chosen: A′: eviction takes the earliest-sent background entry; marking doesn't reorder; running count, no rescan; 10,000-entry test

findings.title: A reconnect with many background entries floods the shared write queue through `fail_all`
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: an install where an app holds thousands of long-running calls. `fail_all` runs synchronously from reconnect cleanup and teardown and would now call one resolve callback per background entry, each enqueuing an update. Thousands of updates in one tick against a 2000-item queue shared with executions, logs and heartbeats overflow it. The overflow is counted, but it also drops unrelated telemetry for that window, and the rows it drops are left to D9. Separately, `fail_all` promises it "never blocks the caller's own cleanup", and today that covers only `set_exception`. A raising callback would abort the loop before the table is cleared.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a reconnect with more background entries than free queue slots drops the excess updates (counted) and leaves those rows to D9's sweep. State in D2 that `fail_all` runs each resolve callback under the same `suppress(Exception)` it uses for `set_exception`.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation

findings.title: The startup sweep scans `api_writes`, and nothing indexes `outcome`
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: a busy install with many writes per day and a long retention window. D3's indexes cover `write_id`, `execution_id`, `context_id`, `sent_ts` and `(app_key, sent_ts)`, not `outcome`. The startup sweep runs through `submit` on the single writer and scans the table. Startup waits on it, and the cost grows with `retention_days` (default 30) times the write rate.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: the startup sweep scans `api_writes` in full, which costs little at the write volumes this project expects.
findings.chosen: A: Add a partial index on pending rows in migration 024
findings.choice_reason: user asked why the sweep should scan the whole table at all
